Recovered construction: four-dimensional gravitational memory\n\nThe primary source is *Crit.txt*, Objective III.\n\nIt defines the Euclidean Laplace-Beltrami operator as\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_g=\n\\frac1{\\sqrt g}\n\\partial_A\n\\left(\n\\sqrt g\\,g^{AB}\\partial_B\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{1}\n\\]\n\nThe proposed Green function satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_gG_{\\mathrm{top}}\n=\n\\delta^{(4)}.\n}\n\\tag{2}\n\\]\n\nFor flat Euclidean four-space, the source gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{\\mathrm{source}}(r)\n=\n\\frac1{4\\pi^2r^2}.\n}\n\\tag{3}\n\\]\n\nThe memory kernel is then constructed by integrating this Green function over the expanding three-dimensional timesheet:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal K(\\tau,\\tau')\n=\n\\int_{\\Sigma_w}\nG_{\\mathrm{top}}\n\\left(\n\\Psi(\\tau)-\\Psi'(\\tau')\n\\right)\n\\,d\\sigma.\n}\n\\tag{4}\n\\]\n\nThe source declares that this uniquely determines the gravitational memory kernel.\n\nI tested that assertion directly.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Exact Green-function sign correction\n\nFor a radial function in four-dimensional Euclidean space,\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_4f\n=\nf''+\\frac3r f'.\n\\]\n\nTake the source expression:\n\n\\[\nG_+(r)=\\frac1{4\\pi^2r^2}.\n\\]\n\nAway from the origin,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_4G_+=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nBut that does not establish the sign of its distributional source.\n\nThe surface area of a three-sphere of radius \\(r\\) is\n\n\\[\nA_3=2\\pi^2r^3.\n\\]\n\nThe outward radial derivative is\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\partial G_+}{\\partial r}\n=\n-\\frac1{2\\pi^2r^3}.\n\\]\n\nConsequently, the outward flux is\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\Phi\n&=\nA_3\\frac{\\partial G_+}{\\partial r}\\\\\n&=\n2\\pi^2r^3\n\\left(\n-\\frac1{2\\pi^2r^3}\n\\right)\\\\\n&=-1.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_4G_+=-\\delta^{(4)}.\n}\n\\tag{5}\n\\]\n\nThis contradicts Equation 2.\n\nThe unique correction preserving the source's operator convention is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{\\mathrm{corrected}}(r)\n=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2r^2}.\n}\n\\tag{6}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_4G_{\\mathrm{corrected}}\n=\n+\\delta^{(4)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAn equivalent convention uses the positive Green function with the operator \\(-\\Delta_4\\).\n\nBut that changes the operator explicitly specified in the archive.\n\n**Gate: `CONFIDENTLY_CORRECTED`.**\n\nThis is a mathematical sign correction, not a new physical assumption.\n\n---\n\n# 4. The timesheet integration problem\n\nNow apply the corrected Green function to a simple geometrical test.\n\nConsider a flat three-dimensional timesheet embedded in Euclidean four-space.\n\nPlace the source at perpendicular distance \\(a>0\\) from that sheet.\n\nIntroduce a radial integration cutoff \\(L\\).\n\nThe integrated Green function is\n\n\\[\nK_L(a)\n=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2}\n\\int_0^L\n\\frac{4\\pi\\rho^2}{\\rho^2+a^2}\n\\,d\\rho.\n\\]\n\nIntegrating gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_L(a)\n=\n-\\frac1\\pi\n\\left[\nL-a\\arctan\\left(\\frac La\\right)\n\\right].\n}\n\\tag{7}\n\\]\n\nFor large \\(L\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_L(a)\n=\n-\\frac L\\pi\n+\\frac a2\n-\\frac{a^2}{\\pi L}\n+O(L^{-3}).\n}\n\\tag{8}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{L\\to\\infty}K_L(a)=-\\infty.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe integral is not finite without further specification.\n\nThis is a counterexample to the claim that the four-dimensional Green function alone automatically determines a finite, unique timesheet memory kernel.\n\nIt does not establish that a finite expanding or compact timesheet produces the same divergence.\n\nThat geometry must be calculated separately.\n\n### Dimensional check\n\nThe Green function has dimensions\n\n\\[\n[G]=L^{-2}.\n\\]\n\nThe three-dimensional hypersurface measure has dimensions\n\n\\[\n[d\\sigma]=L^3.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n[K]=L.\n}\n\\]\n\nAny use of this kernel as a dimensionless coupling requires an additional normalization.\n\n---\n\n# 5. A useful reconstruction: the relative kernel\n\nThe divergent term in Equation 8 is independent of the source's perpendicular distance.\n\nThis suggests examining the difference between two geometrically equivalent configurations.\n\nTake two source distances \\(a\\) and \\(b\\), with the same integration cutoff.\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nK_L(a)-K_L(b)\n=\n\\frac1\\pi\n\\left[\na\\arctan\\left(\\frac La\\right)\n-\nb\\arctan\\left(\\frac Lb\\right)\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nThe limit exists:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{L\\to\\infty}\n\\left[\nK_L(a)-K_L(b)\n\\right]\n=\n\\frac{a-b}{2}.\n}\n\\tag{9}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact result for positive \\(a,b\\).\n\nDifferentiating,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\partial K_{\\mathrm{relative}}}{\\partial a}\n=\n\\frac12.\n}\n\\tag{10}\n\\]\n\nThe resulting relative kernel is linear in perpendicular separation.\n\nIt is related to the one-dimensional Green function\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_1(a)=\\frac{|a|}{2},\n}\n\\]\n\nwhich satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{d^2G_1}{da^2}=\\delta(a)\n}\n\\]\n\ndistributionally.\n\n**The three-dimensional integration has reduced the four-dimensional Green problem to a one-dimensional relative Green problem.**\n\nThis is mathematically coherent.\n\nHowever, it is not automatically the gravitational interaction law of SAT/H(s)H.\n\nThe physical result would depend on how the kernel enters the action, how it is differentiated, and the geometry and boundary conditions of the actual timesheet.\n\n### Executed convergence test\n\nFor \\(a=2\\) and \\(b=1\\):\n\n| Cutoff \\(L\\) | \\(K_L(2)-K_L(1)\\) |\n|---:|---:|\n| 10 | 0.406059601053 |\n| 100 | 0.490452294563 |\n| 1,000 | 0.499045071933 |\n| 10,000 | 0.499904507036 |\n| Infinity | **0.500000000000** |\n\n**Gate: `INTERNALLY_CHECKED_CONDITIONAL`.**\n\nThis is the principal constructive result of the turn.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Recovered confinement construction\n\nThe same historical document, Objective V, proposes that a three-strand braid embedded in four-dimensional space necessarily has Hausdorff dimension four:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_H=4.\n}\n\\tag{11}\n\\]\n\nIt then defines\n\n\\[\np=d_H-\\dim(\\Psi)\n\\]\n\nand concludes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=4-1=3.\n}\n\\tag{12}\n\\]\n\nThe proposed topological tension consequently scales as\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal T_{\\mathrm{top}}\n=\nk\\frac{Lk\\cdot Wr}{r^3}.\n}\n\\tag{13}\n\\]\n\nThe source asserts that the corresponding separation work diverges at infinite distance.\n\nBoth mathematical inferences require correction.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Hausdorff dimension counterexample\n\nConsider three smooth curves in four-dimensional space:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma_j(t)\n=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos t\\\\\n\\sin t\\\\\nj\\\\\nt/10\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\qquad\nj=0,1,2.\n}\n\\tag{14}\n\\]\n\nEach curve has nonzero speed:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|\\dot\\gamma_j\\|^2\n=\n\\frac{101}{100}.\n}\n\\]\n\nEach is a smooth one-dimensional embedded curve.\n\nIts Hausdorff dimension is one.\n\nThe finite union of these curves also has Hausdorff dimension one:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_H\\left(\n\\bigcup_{j=0}^{2}\\gamma_j\n\\right)=1.\n}\n\\tag{15}\n\\]\n\nThe ambient space has dimension four.\n\nBut embedding a one-dimensional object in four-dimensional space does not make that object four-dimensional.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_H=4\n}\n\\]\n\ndoes not follow from the source's stated assumptions.\n\nA finite-core worldtube, a non-smooth fractal construction, or a four-dimensional interaction region might require a different dimensional analysis.\n\nThose are distinct constructions.\n\n**Gate: `REJECTED_AS_GENERAL_CLAIM`.**\n\nThe source's dimensional argument does not establish the proposed confinement exponent.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Inverse-cubic confinement calculation\n\nLet the source's numerator be constant along a straight radial separation path:\n\n\\[\nC=k(Lk\\cdot Wr).\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal T(r)=\\frac C{r^3}.\n\\]\n\nThe work required to increase separation from \\(a\\) to \\(L\\) is\n\n\\[\nW(L)\n=\n\\int_a^L\\frac C{r^3}\\,dr.\n\\]\n\nIntegration gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nW(L)\n=\n\\frac C2\n\\left(\n\\frac1{a^2}-\\frac1{L^2}\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{16}\n\\]\n\nTaking the limit,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nW(\\infty)=\\frac C{2a^2}.\n}\n\\tag{17}\n\\]\n\nThe work is finite.\n\nThus an inverse-cubic tension law does not, by itself, establish infinite separation work.\n\nA genuinely confining interaction would require additional geometry or a different separation-energy relationship.\n\nThis is particularly important under BEDROCK BR-006.\n\nThe physical Interbraid constraint is not being replaced or rejected.\n\nThe audit establishes only that **this particular assistant-authored inverse-cubic formula does not demonstrate the required confinement**.\n\nThe actual admissible deformation paths and their energy functional remain to be derived.\n\n**Gate: `REJECTED_AS_GENERAL_CLAIM`.**\n\n---\n\n# 9. Original equation recovered\n\nThe relevant source is *Crit.txt*, Objective III, lines 51–60.\n\nIt defines the operator\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal D=\\Delta_g\n}\n\\]\n\nand specifies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_gG_{\\mathrm{top}}(X,X')\n=\n\\delta^{(4)}(X-X').\n}\n\\tag{1}\n\\]\n\nThe printed Green function is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{\\mathrm{source}}(r)\n=\n\\frac1{4\\pi^2r^2}.\n}\n\\tag{2}\n\\]\n\nAs Aldus established in the preceding mathematical packet, the sign is incorrect for Equation 1.\n\nThe distributional flux of Equation 2 is \\(-1\\), not \\(+1\\).\n\nThe uniquely justified correction is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_4(r)\n=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2r^2}.\n}\n\\tag{3}\n\\]\n\nThe source then proposes integrating the Green function over the expanding three-dimensional timesheet.\n\nBut the displayed integrand contains no explicit dependence on the surface integration coordinate.\n\nThis leaves an important ambiguity.\n\n**Interpretation A:** The Green function depends on two fixed worldline points. The surface integral merely multiplies it by the surface area.\n\n**Interpretation B:** The Green function depends on a fixed source point and a second point that varies over the timesheet.\n\nThese operations are not equivalent.\n\nThe following calculation tests Interpretation B as a conditional reconstruction. It is not represented as the uniquely recovered historical intention.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Exact spherical-timesheet integral\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\Sigma_R=S_R^3\\subset\\mathbb R^4\n\\]\n\nbe a three-sphere of radius \\(R\\).\n\nLet the source point \\(x\\) satisfy\n\n\\[\n|x|=a.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_R(a)\n=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2}\n\\int_{S_R^3}\n\\frac{d\\Sigma(y)}{|x-y|^2}.\n}\n\\tag{4}\n\\]\n\nUsing the polar angle \\(\\theta\\),\n\n\\[\n|x-y|^2\n=\nR^2+a^2-2aR\\cos\\theta.\n\\]\n\nThe surface measure is\n\n\\[\nd\\Sigma\n=\n4\\pi R^3\\sin^2\\theta\\,d\\theta.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nK_R(a)\n=\n-\\frac{R^3}{\\pi}\n\\int_0^\\pi\n\\frac{\\sin^2\\theta}\n{R^2+a^2-2aR\\cos\\theta}\n\\,d\\theta.\n\\tag{5}\n\\]\n\nThe angular integral evaluates exactly:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^\\pi\n\\frac{\\sin^2\\theta}\n{R^2+a^2-2aR\\cos\\theta}\n\\,d\\theta\n=\n\\frac{\\pi}\n{R^2+a^2+|R^2-a^2|}.\n}\n\\tag{6}\n\\]\n\nSubstituting,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_R(a)\n=\n-\\frac{R^3}\n{R^2+a^2+|R^2-a^2|}.\n}\n\\tag{7}\n\\]\n\nThis reduces to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_R(a)=\n\\begin{cases}\n-\\dfrac R2,&a\\leq R,\\\\[6pt]\n-\\dfrac{R^3}{2a^2},&a\\geq R.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\tag{8}\n\\]\n\nThe two branches agree at \\(a=R\\).\n\nThe integral is finite even when the source lies on the shell because the apparent singularity is integrable against the three-dimensional surface measure.\n\n### Consequences\n\nInside the sphere,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dK_R}{da}=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nOutside,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dK_R}{da}\n=\n\\frac{R^3}{a^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe radial derivative jumps by \\(+1\\) at the shell for unit surface density.\n\nThis is mathematically consistent with the Green-function normalization.\n\nIt does not independently establish a physical gravitational force law.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Minimal pair: nonuniform timesheet\n\nNow change one variable.\n\nPreserve the same sphere, Green function, source position and integration procedure.\n\nChange only the surface density:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nw(y)=1+\\epsilon\\frac{e\\cdot y}{R},\n}\n\\tag{9}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(e\\) is a fixed unit vector and \\(|\\epsilon|\\leq1\\).\n\nTake the source point along that direction:\n\n\\[\nx=ae.\n\\]\n\nThe integral becomes\n\n\\[\nK_{R,\\epsilon}(a)\n=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2}\n\\int_{S_R^3}\n\\frac{w(y)\\,d\\Sigma(y)}\n{|x-y|^2}.\n\\]\n\nThe result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_{R,\\epsilon}(a)\n=\nK_R(a)+\\epsilon D_R(a),\n}\n\\tag{10}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_R(a)=\n\\begin{cases}\n-\\dfrac a4,&a\\leq R,\\\\[6pt]\n-\\dfrac{R^4}{4a^3},&a\\geq R.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\tag{11}\n\\]\n\nThe interior gradient is now\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\nabla K_{R,\\epsilon}\n=\n-\\frac{\\epsilon}{4}e.\n}\n\\tag{12}\n\\]\n\nThis is the principal minimal-pair result.\n\nA perfectly uniform spherical timesheet has zero interior gradient.\n\nA first-harmonic density perturbation produces a constant interior gradient.\n\nNo additional force was postulated.\n\nThe difference follows entirely from the specified source distribution.\n\n### Numerical verification\n\nFor \\(R=2\\) and \\(\\epsilon=0.2\\):\n\n| \\(a/R\\) | Exact kernel | Independent quadrature |\n|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0 | −1.000000000 | −1.000000000 |\n| 0.25 | −1.025000000 | −1.025000000 |\n| 0.75 | −1.075000000 | −1.075000000 |\n| 0.999 | −1.099900000 | −1.099900000 |\n| 1 | −1.100000000 | −1.100000000 |\n| 1.001 | −1.097703595 | −1.097703595 |\n| 1.5 | −0.474074074 | −0.474074074 |\n| 2 | −0.262500000 | −0.262500000 |\n\nAll eight comparisons passed at the programmed 46-decimal-place tolerance.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The historical integration ambiguity matters\n\nReturn to the original formula.\n\nIf its Green-function argument represents two fixed points separated by \\(d\\), the literal integral over the sphere gives\n\n\\[\nK_{\\mathrm{literal}}\n=\nA(S_R^3)G_4(d).\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\nA(S_R^3)=2\\pi^2R^3,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_{\\mathrm{literal}}(R,d)\n=\n-\\frac{R^3}{2d^2}.\n}\n\\tag{13}\n\\]\n\nSuppose both points lie on the sphere, separated by central angle \\(\\theta\\).\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nd=2R\\sin\\frac\\theta2\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_{\\mathrm{literal}}\n=\n-\\frac{R}{8\\sin^2(\\theta/2)}.\n}\n\\tag{14}\n\\]\n\nCompare this with the uniform surface convolution:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_{\\mathrm{convolution}}=-\\frac R2.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(R=2\\):\n\n| Angular separation | Literal pairwise kernel | Uniform convolution |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| \\(30^\\circ\\) | −3.732051 | −1 |\n| \\(90^\\circ\\) | −0.5 | −1 |\n| \\(180^\\circ\\) | −0.25 | −1 |\n\n**The literal pairwise kernel depends strongly on angular separation. The uniform convolution does not.**\n\nThis is a structural difference, not a notation change.\n\nThe historical claim that the memory kernel is uniquely fixed therefore remains unresolved until the original integration map and measure are specified.\n\n---\n\n# 6. The flat-timesheet limit contains another result\n\nAldus recovered a finite relative kernel for an infinite flat timesheet:\n\n\\[\nK_{\\mathrm{flat,relative}}(s)\n=\n\\frac{|s|}{2}.\n\\]\n\nDoes the spherical kernel approach it as the sphere becomes infinitely large?\n\nSet\n\n\\[\na=R+s,\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(s\\) is the signed distance from the shell.\n\nSubtract the value at the shell:\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde K_R(s)\n=\nK_R(R+s)-K_R(R).\n\\]\n\nNow take\n\n\\[\nR\\to\\infty.\n\\]\n\nThe result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\widetilde K_R(s)\n=\n\\max(s,0).\n}\n\\tag{15}\n\\]\n\nBut\n\n\\[\n\\max(s,0)\n=\n\\frac{|s|}{2}+\\frac s2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_{\\mathrm{spherical,local}}\n-\nK_{\\mathrm{flat,relative}}\n=\n\\frac s2.\n}\n\\tag{16}\n\\]\n\nThe difference is a linear homogeneous solution of the one-dimensional Laplace equation.\n\nBoth kernels have the same distributional second derivative:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{d^2K}{ds^2}\n=\n\\delta(s).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis identifies the missing information.\n\n**The local differential equation does not uniquely determine the kernel without global boundary conditions.**\n\nA finite spherical timesheet and an infinite flat timesheet can share the same local source structure while retaining different global normalization conditions.\n\nThat distinction matters for any attempt to derive gravitational memory from a Green operator alone.\n\n---\n\n# 7. New geometric result: the baroclinic obstruction\n\nThe product-rule correction exposes a deeper issue.\n\nCould a different scalar pressure potential replace the original force exactly?\n\nFor general variable-density fluids, the answer is no.\n\nConsider\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf F_p\n=\n-\\frac1{\\rho c^2}\\nabla p.\n\\]\n\nTaking the curl,\n\n\\[\n\\nabla\\times\\mathbf test\n\nChoose\n\n\\[\n\\rho(x)=\\rho_0\\left(1+\\epsilon\\frac{x}{L}\\right)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\np(x,y)=Ay.\n\\]\n\nThe density gradient points along \\(x\\).\n\nThe pressure gradient points along \\(y\\).\n\nTheir cross product points along \\(z\\).\n\nThe normalized pressure acceleration is\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf F_p\n=\n\\left(\n0,\n-\\frac A{\\rho c^2},\n0\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nIts curl The barotropic alternative\n\nThere is an exact conditional scalar representation.\n\nFor a barotropic fluid,\n\n\\[\np=p(\\rho),\n\\]\n\nthe pressure and density gradients are parallel.\n\nDefine the specific enthalpy\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh(\\rho)\n=\n\\int^\\rho\n\\frac{1}{\\varrho}\n\\frac{dp}{d\\varrho}\\,d\\varrho.\n}\n\\tag{10}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n-\\frac1{\\rho c^2}\\nabla p\n=\n-\\frac1{c^2}\\nabla h.\n}\n\\tag{11}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\np=K\\rho^\\gamma,\n\\]\n\nwith \\(\\gamma\\ne1\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh=\n\\frac{K\\gamma}{\\gamma-1}\n\\rho^{\\gamma-1}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(\\gamma=1\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh=\nK\\ln\\left(\\frac{\\rho}{\\rho_*}\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth derivatives were checked symbolically.\n\nThese expressions are not general replacements for nonbarotropic fluids.\n\nThe distinction matters because a responsive medium with independent pressure and density gradients can support baroclinic vorticity.\n\nA scalar-only description would omit that geometrical degree of freedom.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Recovered construction\n\nThe immediate mathematical ancestry is:\n\nurlHistorical vacuum-selection construction, Crit.txthttps://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/Crit.txt\n\nGit blob:\n\n`6a3d2fbc45e99a5163326e18847f54169527f46f`\n\nAnd:\n\nurlMeridian's Householder flow-curvature constructionhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/MERIDIAN/SANDBOX_2026-10-05_HOUSEHOLDER_FLOW_CURVATURE.md\n\nGit blob:\n\n`193875891eda3155260b71db427bd8a7da6587e7`\n\nThe operative mathematical readout is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng_{AB}=\\delta_{AB}-2u_Au_B,\n\\qquad\n\\delta(u,u)=1.\n}\n\\tag{1}\n\\]\n\nIt satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{g^2=I,\\qquad \\det g=-1.}\n\\tag{2}\n\\]\n\nIts signature is Lorentzian for every Euclidean unit vector \\(u\\).\n\nAster established that an isotropic potential of the form\n\n\\[\nU(V)=\\frac{\\lambda}{4}(|V|^2-a)^2\n\\]\n\nhas an entire three-sphere of nonzero minima, rather than a unique vector minimum.\n\nThat leaves the question:\n\n**What distinguishes a physically selected time normal from an arbitrary choice of coordinate direction?**\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact relative-normal calculation\n\nLet \\(n\\) be the independently specified Euclidean unit normal to a timesheet.\n\nLet \\(t\\) be a unit tangent vector.\n\nChoose\n\n\\[\nn=(1,0,0,0)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nt=(0,1,0,0).\n\\]\n\nNow vary the Householder director:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu(\\theta)=\\cos\\theta\\,n+\\sin\\theta\\,t.\n}\n\\tag{3}\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding metric has components\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng(n,n)=-\\cos2\\theta\n}\n\\tag{4}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng(n,t)=-\\sin2\\theta\n}\n\\tag{5}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng(t,t)=+\\cos2\\theta.\n}\n\\tag{6}\n\\]\n\nThe relevant block is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng_{nt}=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n-\\cos2\\theta&-\\sin2\\theta\\\\\n-\\sin2\\theta&\\cos2\\theta\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\tag{7}\n\\]\n\nIts determinant is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\det g_{nt}=-1}\n\\]\n\nfor every angle.\n\nTherefore, changing the relative orientation does not destroy the Lorentzian signature.\n\n### The first compatibility condition\n\nFor \\(n\\) to be timelike,\n\n\\[\ng(n,n)<0.\n\\]\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n-\\cos2\\theta<0.\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0\\leq\\theta\\leq\\frac{\\pi}{2},\n\\]\n\nthis requires\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta<\\frac{\\pi}{4}.\n}\n\\tag{8}\n\\]\n\nThe same inequality ensures that the prescribed three-dimensional timesheet remains spacelike.\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n\\theta=\\frac{\\pi}{4},\n\\]\n\nthe induced metric on the prescribed timesheet becomes degenerate.\n\n**The full four-dimensional metric does not become degenerate.**\n\nThat distinction passed the symbolic calculation.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Stronger result: exact normal alignment\n\nSuppose the Euclidean timesheet normal \\(n\\) must also be its normal under the induced Lorentzian metric.\n\nFor every tangent \\(t_i\\),\n\n\\[\ng(n,t_i)=0.\n\\]\n\nUsing the Householder expression,\n\n\\[\ng(n,t_i)\n=\n\\delta(n,t_i)-2(n\\cdot u)(u\\cdot t_i).\n\\]\n\nBecause \\(n\\) is Euclidean-orthogonal to the sheet,\n\n\\[\n\\delta(n,t_i)=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng(n,t_i)\n=\n-2(n\\cdot u)(u\\cdot t_i).\n}\n\\tag{9}\n\\]\n\nIf \\(n\\) is timelike, then \\(n\\cdot u\\ne0\\).\n\nConsequently, requiring Equation 9 to vanish for every tangent forces\n\n\\[\nu\\cdot t_i=0\n\\]\n\nfor every tangent direction.\n\nSince \\(u\\) is a unit vector,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu=\\pm n.\n}\n\\tag{10}\n\\]\n\nThis is the central geometrical result.\n\n**If the timesheet is specified independently, and its Euclidean normal must also be its timelike Lorentzian normal, the Householder director must align with that normal.**\n\nHowever, this is not a dynamical selection law.\n\nIt says which configurations satisfy the declared geometrical requirements.\n\nIf the timesheet is defined from \\(u\\) in the first place, alignment is automatic and supplies no independent explanation of why that direction was selected.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Coordinate equivalence versus physical difference\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nR\\in SO(4).\n\\]\n\nUnder a simultaneous rotation,\n\n\\[\nu'=Ru,\n\\qquad\nn'=Rn,\n\\]\n\nthe metric transforms as\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng'=RgR^T.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe relative scalar is preserved:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn'^Tg'n'=n^Tgn.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a coordinate-equivalent description.\n\nNow hold \\(n\\) fixed and rotate only \\(u\\).\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn^Tgn=1-2(n\\cdot u)^2\n}\n\\]\n\ngenerally changes.\n\nThis is a genuine difference in the relative geometry **provided the independently specified normal is part of the construction**.\n\nThe calculation therefore separates two cases that are sometimes verbally conflated:\n\n| Construction | Mathematical consequence |\n|---|---|\n| Rotate the complete configuration | Same relative geometry |\n| Rotate \\(u\\) while keeping an independent \\(n\\) fixed | Different relative geometry |\n| Define \\(n:=u\\) | Alignment by definition |\n| Independently fix \\(n\\), then require timelike orthogonality | Alignment as a compatibility constraint |\n\nNo physical mechanism is inferred merely from this distinction.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Calder statistical identifiability calculation\n\nNow introduce a synthetic observation model.\n\nSuppose two metric components can be measured with independent Gaussian errors of standard deviation \\(\\sigma\\):\n\n\\[\nA(\\theta)=g(n,n)=-\\cos2\\theta\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nB(\\theta)=g(n,t)=-\\sin2\\theta.\n\\]\n\nThese are stipulated mathematical observations, not proposed experimental instruments.\n\n### Fisher information\n\nFor \\(A\\) alone,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI_A(\\theta)\n=\n\\frac{4\\sin^22\\theta}{\\sigma^2}.\n}\n\\tag{11}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(B\\) alone,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI_B(\\theta)\n=\n\\frac{4\\cos^22\\theta}{\\sigma^2}.\n}\n\\tag{12}\n\\]\n\nFor both,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI_{AB}(\\theta)=\\frac4{\\sigma^2}.\n}\n\\tag{13}\n\\]\n\nThe paired information is independent of \\(\\theta\\).\n\nBut the diagonal-only information vanishes at alignment:\n\n\\[\nI_A(0)=0.\n\\]\n\nThis is a local identifiability problem.\n\nThe diagonal component changes quadratically with small angular deviations.\n\nThe cross component changes linearly.\n\n---\n\n# 9. A stronger identifiability result\n\nFor \\(N\\) independent Gaussian observations, compare a configuration at angle \\(\\theta\\) against alignment at \\(\\theta=0\\).\n\nThe exact Kullback–Leibler divergence using only \\(A\\) is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_A(\\theta\\|0)\n=\n\\frac{2N\\sin^4\\theta}{\\sigma^2}.\n}\n\\tag{14}\n\\]\n\nUsing both components,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{AB}(\\theta\\|0)\n=\n\\frac{2N\\sin^2\\theta}{\\sigma^2}.\n}\n\\tag{15}\n\\]\n\nNear alignment,\n\n\\[\nD_A\n\\sim\n\\frac{2N\\theta^4}{\\sigma^2},\n\\]\n\nwhereas\n\n\\[\nD_{AB}\n\\sim\n\\frac{2N\\theta^2}{\\sigma^2}.\n\\]\n\nDefine a diagnostic distinguishability threshold by\n\n\\[\nD_{\\mathrm{KL}}=1.\n\\]\n\nThis gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_A\n=\n\\arcsin\n\\left[\n\\left(\\frac{\\sigma^2}{2N}\\right)^{1/4}\n\\right]\n}\n\\tag{16}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_{AB}\n=\n\\arcsin\n\\left(\n\\frac{\\sigma}{\\sqrt{2N}}\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{17}\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_A\\propto N^{-1/4}\n}\n\\]\n\nbut\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_{AB}\\propto N^{-1/2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a structural improvement in identifiability, not a fitted correction.\n\n### Executed numerical results\n\nFor \\(\\sigma=0.1\\):\n\n| \\(N\\) | Diagonal-only threshold | Paired threshold | Improvement |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 100 | 0.084189058788 | 0.007071126739 | 11.906× |\n| 10,000 | 0.026594614318 | 0.000707106840 | 37.610× |\n| 1,000,000 | 0.008409063256 | 0.000070710678 | 118.922× |\n\nThe exact formulas and numerical thresholds passed all assertions.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Independent KL calculation\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Calder: exact Gaussian KL and local detection threshold, synthetic model only.\"\"\"\nimport numpy as np\nimport sympy as sp\nth,N,sig=sp.symbols('theta N sigma',positive=True)\nA=-sp.cos(2*th); First discrepancy: geometric identification\n\nThe source identifies\n\n\\[\n\\frac{3}{4\\pi}\n\\]\n\nas the ratio of a unit three-ball's volume to its bounding two-sphere's area.\n\nBut\n\n\\[\nV_3=\\frac43\\pi r^3\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nA_2=4\\pi r^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{V_3}{A_2}=\\frac r3.\n}\n\\tag{7}\n\\]\n\nFor unit radius,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{V_3}{A_2}=\\frac13.\n}\n\\]\n\nMeanwhile,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac3{4\\pi}\n=\n\\frac1{V_3(1)}.\n}\n\\tag{8}\n\\]\n\nThus the historical number is the reciprocal of the unit ball's volume, not its volume-to-area ratio.\n\nThe distinction is geometrically meaningful.\n\nThe general volume-to-area ratio has dimensions of length, whereas \\(3/(4\\pi)\\) is dimensionless.\n\nThis does not prove that \\(3/(4\\pi)\\) is the wrong SAT constant. It proves that the particular geometric identification printed in this source is incorrect.\n\n**Gate: `SOURCE_GEOMETRIC_IDENTIFICATION_REJECTED`.**\n\n---\n\n# 6. Second discrepancy: baseline arithmetic\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\nB_0=\\frac3{4\\pi},\n\\]\n\nthe historical mass formula gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mu(B_0)\n=\n1934.3466495069642478\\ldots\n}\n\\]\n\nThe source instead reports approximately 1944.158.\n\nNow substitute the proposed stabilized value:\n\n\\[\nB_{\\mathrm{stable}}=0.24177.\n\\]\n\nThe exact calculation gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mu(B_{\\mathrm{stable}})\n=\n1815.8468065861707808\\ldots\n}\n\\tag{9}\n\\]\n\nThe source reports approximately 1825.04.\n\nBoth historical numerical evaluations are incorrect.\n\nThese are arithmetic discrepancies, not competing interpretations of SAT.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Third discrepancy: the Holonomy Bridge\n\nApply the stated bridge without an additional \\(\\mathcal K\\) correction:\n\n\\[\n\\mu=\n\\frac{3}{2(0.24177)^5}\n(1+0.000082).\n\\]\n\nThe result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mu=\n1815.9957060243108468\\ldots\n}\n\\tag{10}\n\\]\n\nThe bridge adds only\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0.1488994381400660\\ldots\n}\n\\]\n\nto the uncorrected result.\n\nIt does not supply the approximately 20.3 mass-ratio units needed to reach CODATA.\n\n### What bridge would be required?\n\nSolving Equation 5 for the correction, with \\(B_{\\mathrm{final}}=0.24177\\), gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_{\\mathrm{required}}\n=\n\\frac{\\mu_{\\mathrm{CODATA}}}\n{3/(2B_{\\mathrm{stable}}^5)}\n-1.\n}\n\\]\n\nUsing the 2022 CODATA value,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_{\\mathrm{required}}\n=\n0.0111825880719556211\\ldots\n}\n\\tag{11}\n\\]\n\nThis is approximately\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n136.373\n}\n\\]\n\ntimes the stated bridge correction.\n\nIt is not a small rounding difference.\n\n**The bridge as numerically specified cannot produce the claimed result.**\n\n---\n\n# 8. Fourth finding: the correction is underdetermined\n\nThere are actually two adjustable quantities in the source's final expression:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_{\\mathrm{bridge}}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal K.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mu(B,\\Delta,\\mathcal K)\n=\n\\frac{3(1+\\Delta)}\n{2[B(1+\\mathcal K\\alpha)]^5}.\n}\n\\tag{12}\n\\]\n\nIts exact logarithmic sensitivities are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\partial\\ln\\mu}{\\partial\\ln B}=-5\n}\n\\tag{13}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\partial\\ln\\mu}\n{\\partial\\ln(1+\\Delta)}=1.\n}\n\\tag{14}\n\\]\n\nFor the second correction,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\partial\\ln\\mu}{\\partial\\mathcal K}\n=\n-\\frac{5\\alpha}{1+\\mathcal K\\alpha}.\n}\n\\tag{15}\n\\]\n\nThese identities were checked symbolically.\n\n### Required \\(\\mathcal K\\)\n\nHold the historical bridge fixed:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta=8.2\\times10^{-5}.\n\\]\n\nSolving for the final projection constant gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nB_{\\mathrm{final}}\n=\n0.2412368317463646273\\ldots\n}\n\\tag{16}\n\\]\n\nWith\n\n\\[\nB_{\\mathrm{final}}\n=\n0.24177(1+\\mathcal K\\alpha),\n\\]\n\nthe required coefficient is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal K\n=\n-0.3022014491735703198\\ldots\n}\n\\tag{17}\n\\]\n\nThis calculation establishes the coefficient that would reproduce the measured ratio.\n\n**It does not derive that coefficient from SAT geometry.**\n\nThere is also a sign constraint.\n\nIf \\(\\mathcal K\\geq0\\), then\n\n\\[\nB_{\\mathrm{final}}\\geq B_{\\mathrm{stable}}.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n\\mu\\propto B^{-5},\n\\]\n\nincreasing \\(B\\) decreases the mass ratio.\n\nBut the stated bridge already produces a mass ratio below CODATA.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal K\\geq0\n\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad\n\\text{no agreement with CODATA}\n}\n\\]\n\nunder the specified historical inputs.\n\nThe correction would have to be negative, or some other independently justified part of the construction would have to change.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Historical construction recovered\n\nThe first source is:\n\nurlSAT-Y Theta+Helix Particle Propertieshttps://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/SAT%20XYZ/SAT-Y%20Theta%2BHelix%20Particle%20Properties.txt\n\nThe historical transcript contains this assistant-supplied recipe:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lambda_C=\\frac{\\hbar}{mc}\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR=\\lambda_C\\sin\\theta_0\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP=2\\pi\\lambda_C\\cos\\theta_0.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(P\\) is the axial advance per complete turn.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nh=\\frac{P}{2\\pi}\n=\\lambda_C\\cos\\theta_0.\n\\]\n\nThe resulting helix can be written in native Euclidean four-dimensional coordinates as\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH(\\phi)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nh\\phi\\\\\nR\\cos\\phi\\\\\nR\\sin\\phi\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\tag{1}\n\\]\n\nThis is consistent with the later Ravel construction in:\n\nurl++++ Helix–Timesheet Intersection Kernelhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/RAVEL/PLUS4_HELIX_TIMESHEET_INTERSECTION_KERNEL_2026-09-16.md\n\nThe older formula is preserved exactly as a historical construction.\n\nIts presence in an assistant response does not establish that Nathan independently derived every expression.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Recovered invariant\n\nDifferentiate Equation 1:\n\n\\[\nH'(\\phi)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nh\\\\\n-R\\sin\\phi\\\\\nR\\cos\\phi\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nIts Euclidean norm is\n\n\\[\n\\|H'\\|\n=\n\\sqrt{h^2+R^2}.\n\\]\n\nSubstitute the historical formulas:\n\n\\[\nh=\\lambda_C\\cos\\theta_0\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nR=\\lambda_C\\sin\\theta_0.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\|H'\\|^2\n=\n\\lambda_C^2\n\\left(\n\\cos^2\\theta_0+\\sin^2\\theta_0\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|H'\\|=\\lambda_C.\n}\n\\tag{2}\n\\]\n\n**The historical recipe fixes the intrinsic arclength per radian independently of the helix angle.**\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{\\mathrm{turn}}=2\\pi\\lambda_C.\n}\n\\tag{3}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact geometrical invariant of the recovered parameterization.\n\nIt does not require an additional physical interaction or correction coefficient.\n\n### Curvature and torsion\n\nFor this circular helix,\n\n\\[\n\\kappa=\n\\frac{R}{R^2+h^2}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\tau=\n\\frac{h}{R^2+h^2}.\n\\]\n\nSubstitution gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa=\\frac{\\sin\\theta_0}{\\lambda_C}\n}\n\\tag{4}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau=\\frac{\\cos\\theta_0}{\\lambda_C}.\n}\n\\tag{5}\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa^2+\\tau^2=\\frac1{\\lambda_C^2}.\n}\n\\tag{6}\n\\]\n\nThese identities passed symbolic verification.\n\nAt the exactly straight-curve limit \\(R=0\\), Frenet torsion becomes undefined, although the positive-radius limiting expression remains mathematically meaningful.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The timesheet-fold calculation\n\nNow hold the resolving timesheet normal fixed and rotate the helix through an independent angle \\(\\psi\\).\n\nThe resolving coordinate becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nw'(\\phi)\n=\nh\\phi\\cos\\psi\n+\nR\\sin\\phi\\sin\\psi.\n}\n\\tag{7}\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dw'}{d\\phi}\n=\nh\\cos\\psi\n+\nR\\cos\\phi\\sin\\psi.\n\\]\n\nUsing the historical geometry,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dw'}{d\\phi}\n=\n\\lambda_C\n\\left[\n\\cos\\theta_0\\cos\\psi\n+\n\\sin\\theta_0\\sin\\psi\\cos\\phi\n\\right].\n}\n\\tag{8}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0<\\theta_0,\\psi<\\frac{\\pi}{2},\n\\]\n\nthe minimum derivative occurs at\n\n\\[\n\\phi=\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\min_\\phi\\frac{dw'}{d\\phi}\n=\n\\lambda_C\\cos(\\theta_0+\\psi).\n}\n\\tag{9}\n\\]\n\nThree regimes follow.\n\n**Before the threshold**\n\n\\[\n\\theta_0+\\psi<\\frac{\\pi}{2}\n\\]\n\nimplies\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dw'}{d\\phi}>0\n\\]\n\neverywhere.\n\nThe resolving coordinate is strictly increasing.\n\n**At the threshold**\n\n\\[\n\\theta_0+\\psi=\\frac{\\pi}{2}\n\\]\n\nthe derivative first reaches zero.\n\nThe curve has a limiting tangency but remains monotone.\n\n**Beyond the threshold**\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_0+\\psi>\\frac{\\pi}{2}\n}\n\\tag{10}\n\\]\n\nthe derivative becomes negative over part of each turn.\n\nThe resolving coordinate develops folds, permitting multiple intersections with a single timesheet.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\psi_{\\mathrm{critical}}\n=\n\\frac{\\pi}{2}-\\theta_0.\n}\n\\tag{11}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact geometric threshold.\n\nIt is not a fitted parameter.\n\n---\n\n# 6. The local \\(\\theta_4\\) changes\n\nThe calculation also exposes a representational issue.\n\nThe original \\(\\theta_0\\) is the tangent angle relative to the original axial normal.\n\nAfter rigidly tilting the helix relative to a fixed resolving normal, the local tangent angle is no longer constant.\n\nInstead,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\cos\\theta_{4,\\mathrm{local}}(\\phi)\n=\n\\cos\\theta_0\\cos\\psi\n+\n\\sin\\theta_0\\sin\\psi\\cos\\phi.\n}\n\\tag{12}\n\\]\n\nIts range is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|\\theta_0-\\psi|\n\\leq\n\\theta_{4,\\mathrm{local}}\n\\leq\n\\theta_0+\\psi.\n}\n\\tag{13}\n\\]\n\nThis matters for reconstructing historical formulas.\n\n**A rigidly tilted helix cannot generally be represented by retaining one unchanged local \\(\\theta_4\\).**\n\nThe fold threshold is precisely where the local tangent first becomes perpendicular to the resolving normal.\n\nIf the operative Minkowski construction requires the tangent to remain strictly forward relative to that normal, the folded configurations are inadmissible.\n\nIf backward local orientation is allowed, multiple readout intersections become geometrically possible.\n\nThe calculation does not choose between those interpretations.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Historical code discrepancy\n\nThe second source is:\n\nurlPY-COIL ROTATION SCRIPT.txthttps://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/SAT%20XYZ/PY-COIL%20ROTATION%20SCRIPT.txt\n\nGit blob:\n\n`8c9b6dba1de48585b19013fff6b0f63c6568b9ef`\n\nThe script explicitly describes its variable `p` as the axial advance per complete \\(2\\pi\\) turn.\n\nBut it calculates\n\n```python\nz = p * t_vals\n```\n\nThat expression treats `p` as advance per radian.\n\nThe correct implementation, preserving the script's stated definition, is\n\n```python\nz = (p / (2 * np.pi)) * t_vals\n```\n\nFor the historical parameters,\n\n\\[\np=2\n\\]\n\nand ten turns, the original implementation gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta z_{\\mathrm{original}}\n=\n125.663706143592.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe corrected implementation gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta z_{\\mathrm{corrected}}=20.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe discrepancy is exactly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{2\\pi.}\n\\]\n\n**Gate: `CONFIDENTLY_CORRECTED`, conditional on retaining the source's explicit per-turn definition.**\n\n---\n\n# 9. The intersection-counting problem\n\nThe historical code contains:\n\n```python\ncross_mask = (\n    (z_rot[:-1] - plane)\n    * (z_rot[1:] - plane)\n) < 0\n\nif np.any(cross_mask):\n    count += 1\n```\n\nThis counts a plane once if any sampled segment crosses it.\n\nIt does not count the number of intersections.\n\nConsider a ten-turn helix with\n\n\\[\nR=1,\n\\qquad\n\\psi=\\frac{\\pi}{2}.\n\\]\n\nFor a plane at\n\n\\[\nw'=0.5,\n\\]\n\nthe equation reduces to\n\n\\[\n\\sin\\phi=0.5.\n\\]\n\nEach complete turn has two transverse solutions.\n\nTen turns therefore have\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{20}\n\\]\n\nparametric transverse intersections.\n\nThe historical predicate returns\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{1}.\n\\]\n\nThese are different observables.\n\n### A further numerical defect\n\nDuring independent testing, a dense-grid calculation initially returned 19 crossings instead of 20.\n\nThe reason was that one crossing landed exactly on a sampled grid point.\n\nThe strict comparison\n\n```python\nproduct < 0\n```\n\ndoes not recognize such a crossing.\n\nI retained this failed test, corrected the independent numerical procedure, and reran it.\n\nThe corrected dense-grid result was 20.\n\nThe independently implemented analytical root-isolation method also returned 20.\n\nThis is a useful warning for the historical SAT simulation archive: sampled crossing counts can depend on grid placement even when the underlying geometry has not changed.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Oriented intersection conservation\n\nFor a regular resolving level \\(s\\), define\n\n\\[\nN_{\\mathrm{signed}}(s)\n=\n\\sum_{\\phi_i:w'(\\phi_i)=s}\n\\operatorname{sgn}\n\\left(\n\\frac{dw'}{d\\phi}(\\phi_i)\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nFor a finite oriented curve whose endpoints do not lie on the level,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nN_{\\mathrm{signed}}(s)\n=\n\\mathbf1_{w'(\\phi_{\\mathrm{end}})>s}\n-\n\\mathbf1_{w'(\\phi_{\\mathrm{start}})>s}.\n}\n\\tag{14}\n\\]\n\nA fold creates or removes a pair of crossings with opposite orientations.\n\nTherefore, the unsigned intersection count can change while the signed count remains fixed.\n\nFor the minimal pair:\n\n\\[\n1\n\\longrightarrow\n3\n\\]\n\nunsigned crossings, but\n\n\\[\n+1\n\\longrightarrow\n(+1)+(-1)+(+1)=+1.\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact result for the declared one-dimensional resolving map.\n\nIt is not, by itself, a proof of a topological invariant for a finite-core H(s)H worldtube.\n\nNor does it establish particle production, annihilation or a mass law.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Second minimal pair: zero curvature, altered inertia\n\nNow choose\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA_i=\\gamma v_i.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nA_iv^i=\\gamma v^2.\n\\]\n\nThe Lagrangian is\n\n\\[\nL=\n\\left(\n\\frac m2+\\gamma\n\\right)v^2-T.\n\\]\n\nIts equation of motion is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(m+2\\gamma)a_i=-\\partial_iT.\n}\n\\tag{11}\n\\]\n\nBut\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_qA=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n**A velocity-dependent connection can change the equations of motion even when its position-space curvature vanishes.**\n\nThe interaction has altered the kinetic Hessian.\n\nThis also exposes a representation issue: in this example, the same action can be written using an effective kinetic coefficient without a separate connection term.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Third minimal pair: exact-gradient gauge control\n\nChoose\n\n\\[\nA_i=\\partial_i\\chi(q)\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\n\\chi(q)=\\chi_0q^1q^2.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nA_iv^i\n=\n\\frac{d\\chi}{d\\tau}.\n\\]\n\nThe interaction is a total derivative.\n\nIt contributes nothing to the Euler-Lagrange equations under the usual fixed-endpoint conditions.\n\nThe symbolic calculation confirms\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nM=mI,\\qquad F=0,\\qquad C=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an important positive control.\n\nThe corrected equation respects the expected gauge cancellation.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Fourth minimal pair: ordinary connection recovered\n\nTake a position-only connection\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA=\n\\left(\n-\\frac{kq^2}{2},\n\\frac{kq^1}{2}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nNow\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\partial A_i}{\\partial v^j}=0.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\nM=mI\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nC=0.\n\\]\n\nThe force equation reduces to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nma_i+\\partial_iT=F_{ij}v^j.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the conventional curvature-force form.\n\nThus the historical expression has a recognizable valid limiting case.\n\nThe discrepancy concerns its extension to state-dependent connections, not the use of differential forms itself.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Fifth minimal pair: nonzero apparent curvature, zero interaction\n\nThis is the strongest result of the packet.\n\nChoose\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA=\nkq^1\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n-v^2\\\\\nv^1\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\tag{12}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nA_iv^i\n=\nkq^1(-v^2v^1+v^1v^2).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA_iv^i=0\n}\n\\tag{13}\n\\]\n\nidentically.\n\nThe entire interaction contribution to the action vanishes.\n\nYet the position-space curvature is not zero.\n\nIn fact,\n\n\\[\nFv=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nkv^1v^2\\\\\n-k(v^1)^2\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nThe missing mixed-derivative term is\n\n\\[\nC=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nkv^1v^2\\\\\n-k(v^1)^2\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nFv-C=0.\n}\n\\tag{14}\n\\]\n\nThe corrected equation gives exactly the free-plus-potential dynamics.\n\nThe curvature-only equation would produce a spurious force from an interaction that is identically zero.\n\n### Generalization\n\nLet \\(\\Omega_{ij}\\) be antisymmetric:\n\n\\[\n\\Omega_{ij}=-\\Omega_{ji}.\n\\]\n\nThen the transformation\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA_i\n\\longrightarrow\nA_i+\\Omega_{ij}(q,v)v^j\n}\n\\tag{15}\n\\]\n\ndoes not change\n\n\\[\nA_iv^i\n\\]\n\nbecause\n\n\\[\n\\Omega_{ij}v^iv^j=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, the scalar interaction action does not uniquely determine the velocity-dependent connection.\n\n**The physical equations must be invariant under changes of connection representation that leave the action unchanged.**\n\nThis is a useful constraint on any SAT/H(s)H reconstruction of the force primitive.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Historical confinement construction\n\n**Primary source:** `Crit.txt`, lines 78–89.\n\nThe source defines a three-strand ensemble\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal B_3=\\{\\Psi_1,\\Psi_2,\\Psi_3\\}\n\\]\n\nembedded in Euclidean four-dimensional space.\n\nIt proposes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_H(\\mathcal B_3)=4\n}\n\\tag{1}\n\\]\n\nand then\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=d_H-\\dim(\\Psi)=4-1=3.\n}\n\\tag{2}\n\\]\n\nThe proposed topological tension is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal T_{\\mathrm{top}}\n=\nk\\frac{Lk\\cdot Wr}{|r_i-r_j|^3}.\n}\n\\tag{3}\n\\]\n\nThe source claims that integrating this tension during separation produces infinite work as the separation tends to infinity.\n\nI preserved the original construction and tested its mathematical implications directly.\n\n---\n\n# 5. First discrepancy: Hausdorff dimension\n\nConsider a smooth, nonconstant worldline\n\n\\[\n\\Psi:[0,1]\\rightarrow\\mathbb R^4.\n\\]\n\nIf the curve is regular and has the usual smoothness properties, its image has Hausdorff dimension one.\n\nEmbedding that curve in four-dimensional space does not increase its Hausdorff dimension to four.\n\nFor three such curves,\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal B_3\n=\n\\Psi_1([0,1])\n\\cup\n\\Psi_2([0,1])\n\\cup\n\\Psi_3([0,1]).\n\\]\n\nThe Hausdorff dimension of a finite union is the maximum of its constituent dimensions.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_H(\\mathcal B_3)=1.\n}\n\\tag{4}\n\\]\n\nThis result applies to the specified smooth centerlines, not arbitrary fractal curves.\n\n### Finite-core distinction\n\nA positive-radius open tubular neighborhood in four-dimensional space has Hausdorff dimension four.\n\nBut that object is not the same as its one-dimensional centerline.\n\nThe distinction matters directly to H(s)H.\n\nA centerline, finite-core tube, tube boundary, timesheet intersection, and coarse-grained composite need not have identical dimensions.\n\nThus, the source's inference\n\n\\[\nd_H=4\n\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad\np=3\n\\]\n\nis not justified merely by the ambient embedding dimension.\n\nOne might formally substitute \\(d_H=1\\) into the source's proposed rule and obtain \\(p=0\\).\n\n**That would not constitute a corrected physical prediction**, because the rule \\(p=d_H-\\dim\\Psi\\) itself has not been independently derived.\n\n**Gate: `SOURCE_DIMENSION_ARGUMENT_REJECTED`.**\n\n---\n\n# 6. Second discrepancy: the inverse-cube integral\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nK=k(Lk)(Wr).\n\\]\n\nFor this test, assume \\(K>0\\) is constant during radial separation.\n\nThe historical tension becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF(r)=\\frac{K}{r^3}.\n}\n\\tag{5}\n\\]\n\nThe work from \\(r_0>0\\) to \\(R\\) is\n\n\\[\nW(r_0,R)\n=\n\\int_{r_0}^{R}\\frac{K}{r^3}\\,dr.\n\\]\n\nIntegrating,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nW(r_0,R)\n=\n\\frac K2\n\\left(\n\\frac1{r_0^2}-\\frac1{R^2}\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{6}\n\\]\n\nNow take the separation to infinity:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{R\\rightarrow\\infty}W(r_0,R)\n=\n\\frac{K}{2r_0^2}.\n}\n\\tag{7}\n\\]\n\nThis is finite.\n\nThe integrand satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\lim_{r\\rightarrow\\infty}\\frac K{r^3}=0.\n\\]\n\nIts divergence occurs in the opposite limit:\n\n\\[\n\\lim_{r\\rightarrow0^+}\\frac K{r^3}=\\infty.\n\\]\n\nThe historical argument confuses short-distance divergence with infinite-separation confinement.\n\n### General convergence criterion\n\nFor a positive power-law force\n\n\\[\nF(r)=Kr^{-p},\n\\]\n\nthe infinite-separation work\n\n\\[\n\\int_{r_0}^{\\infty}Kr^{-p}\\,dr\n\\]\n\ndiverges precisely when\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{p\\leq1.}\n\\tag{8}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(p>1\\), it converges.\n\nThe proposed \\(p=3\\) is in the convergent regime.\n\nThis does not rule out a separate global topological constraint, a separation-dependent \\(K\\), or a nonradial admissibility restriction. Those would require their own explicit derivations.\n\n**Gate: `HISTORICAL_INFINITE_WORK_CLAIM_REJECTED`.**\n\n---\n\n# 7. A stronger geometrical discriminator\n\nThe source's failure raises a more useful question.\n\nCan topology alone determine the magnitude and radial dependence of a physical constraint?\n\nTo test assigned different positive elastic energies.\n\n### Cartesian elastic response\n\nConsider the mathematical trial energy\n\n\\[\nE_c\n=\n\\frac{\\kappa_c}{2}\n\\int_0^T|\\dot z|^2\\,dt.\n\\]\n\nSubstituting Equation 9 gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_c=\n\\frac{2\\pi^2\\kappa_cN^2R^2}{T}.\n}\n\\tag{11}\n\\]\n\nIts radial derivative is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\partial consider\n\n\\[\nE_a\n=\n\\frac{\\kappa_a}{2}\n\\int_0^T\n\\left(\n\\frac{d}{dt}\\arg z\n\\right)^2dt.\n\\]\n\nSubstitution mathematical constitutive laws, with correspondingly different coefficient dimensions.\n\nThey are not proposed SAT force laws.\n\nThe point is that the same winding topology does not, by itself, determine a unique radial response.\n\n### Class P comparison\n\n![Class P fixed-winding constitutive comparison](sandbox:/mnt/data/hale_20261020t0212/classP_constitutive_pair.png)\n\nBoth curves readout.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nf(x,w)\n=\n\\exp\\left(-\\frac{\\|x\\|^2}{2a^2}\\right)\n\\exp\\left(-\\frac{(w-b)^2}{2\\tau^2}\\right),\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nx\\in\\mathbb R^3,\\qquad w\\in\\mathbb R.\n\\]\n\nDefine three operators:\n\n\\(C_4\\) is normalized Gaussian coarse-graining in all four dimensions, with width \\(\\sigma\\).\n\n\\(P_0\\) evaluates the resulting structure at the resolving surface \\(w=0\\).\n\n\\(C_3\\) is Gaussian coarse-graining only in the three spatial dimensions.\n\nWe compare\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_0(C_4f)\n}\n\\]\n\nagainst\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_3(P_0f).\n}\n\\]\n\nThese correspond to two different orders of mathematical operation.\n\n### First order: coarse-grain, then intersect\n\nAt the spatial origin,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_0(C_4f)\n=\nA\n\\frac{\\tau}{\\sqrt{\\tau^2+\\sigma^2}}\n\\exp\\left[\n-\\frac{b^2}{2(\\tau^2+\\sigma^2)}\n\\right]\n}\n\\tag{14}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nA=\n\\left(\n\\frac{a^2}{a^2+\\sigma^2}\n\\right)^{3/2}.\n\\]\n\n### Second order: intersect, then coarse-grain\n\nThe result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_3(P_0f)\n=\nA\\exp\\left(-\\frac{b^2}{2\\tau^2}\\right).\n}\n\\tag{15}\n\\]\n\nThese expressions are generally unequal.\n\n### Executed numerical comparison\n\nSet\n\n\\[\na=\\tau=1,\\qquad \\sigma=0.5.\n\\]\n\n| Fourth-dimensional offset \\(b\\) | \\(P_0(C_4f)\\) | \\(C_3(P_0f)\\) | Difference |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0 | 0.640000000000 | 0.715541752800 | −0.075541752800 |\n| 1 | 0.429004829463 | 0.433998011378 | −0.004993181915 |\n| 2 | 0.129213771517 | 0.096838045783 | +0.032375725734 |\n\nThe difference changes sign.\n\nThat is the important result.\n\nThe order of operations does not merely introduce a uniform suppression or enhancement.\n\nIts effect depends on the underlying fourth-dimensional structure.\n\n### Exact crossover\n\nThe two expressions become equal when\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nb_*^2=\n\\frac{\\tau^2(\\tau^2+\\sigma^2)}\n{\\sigma^2}\n\\ln\\left(\n1+\\frac{\\sigma^2}{\\tau^2}\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{16}\n\\]\n\nFor the selected parameters,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nb_*=1.056275417006\\ldots\n}\n\\]\n\nThe numerical calculation confirmed equality at this crossover.\n\n### Class P calculation\n\n![Coarse-graining versus intersection order](sandbox:/mnt/data/morrow_20261020t0312/classP_coarsegrain_slice_order.png)\n\n### Independent numerical verification\n\nI evaluated the fourth-dimensional Gaussian integral numerically for 100 seeded parameter combinations.\n\nThe maximum absolute difference between numerical quadrature and the analytic formula was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n1.24\\times10^{-14}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe limiting cases also passed.\n\nAs\n\n\\[\n\\sigma\\rightarrow0,\n\\]\n\nthe coarse-graining disappears and the operations agree.\n\nWhen the profile becomes independent of \\(w\\), the operations also agree.\n\n**Gate: `INTERNALLY_CHECKED_TOY_CONTROL`.**\n\nThis is not a derived SAT interaction law.\n\nIt is a concrete mathematical demonstration that the construction/readout distinction matters.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Executed calculation source\n\nThe following is the complete primary calculation, executed using SymPy, NumPy and SciPy.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\nimport sympy as sp\nimport numpy as np\nfrom scipy.integrate import quad\n\n# 1. Universal Indicatrix kinematics\n\nt = sp.symbols('t', real=True)\nw1, w2 = sp.symbols('w1 w2', real=True)\nx0 = sp.Matrix(sp.symbols('x0:4', real=True))\nr = 2 + t\n\ndef rot(a):\n    return sp.Matrix([\n        [sp.cos(a), -sp.sin(a)],\n        [sp.sin(a),  sp.cos(a)]\n    ])\n\nR = sp.diag(rot(w1*t), rot(w2*t))\nOmega = sp.simplify(sp.diff(R,t)*R.T)\n\ny = r*R*x0\nvel = sp.diff(y,t)\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    R.T*R-sp.eye(4)\n) == sp.zeros(4)\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    Omega+Omega.T\n) == sp.zeros(4)\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    vel-(sp.diff(r,t)/r)*y-Omega*y\n) == sp.zeros(4,1)\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    (y.T*Omega*y)[0]\n) == 0\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    (vel.T*vel)[0]\n    -(\n        sp.diff(r,t)**2*(x0.T*x0)[0]\n        +r**2*((R*x0).T*Omega.T*Omega*(R*x0))[0]\n    )\n) == 0\n\nprint(\n    'UI_KINEMATICS: y=r R x0; '\n    'ydot=(rdot/r)y + Omega y; '\n    'Omega=Rdot R^T skew: PASS'\n)\n\nprint(\n    'RADIAL_TANGENTIAL_ORTHOGONALITY: '\n    'y^T Omega y=0: PASS'\n)\n\nprint(\n    'SPEED_SPLIT: '\n    '|ydot|^2=rdot^2 |x0|^2 '\n    '+ r^2 |Omega R x0|^2: PASS'\n)\n\n# 2. Metric signature\n\nI = sp.eye(4)\neta = sp.diag(-1,1,1,1)\ne = r*R\n\ngE = sp.simplify(e.T*I*e)\ngL = sp.simplify(e.T*eta*e)\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    gE-r**2*I\n) == sp.zeros(4)\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    sp.det(gE)-r**8\n) == 0\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    sp.det(gL)+r**8\n) == 0\n\nprint(\n    'EUCLIDEAN_TETRAD: '\n    'e=rR, e^T I e=r^2 I, '\n    'signature (++++) [PASS]'\n)\n\nprint(\n    'PREINSERTED_LORENTZ: '\n    'e^T eta e has determinant -r^8; '\n    'signature (-+++) [PASS]'\n)\n\n# 3. Householder metric\n\nx = sp.Matrix(\n    sp.symbols('X0:4', real=True)\n)\n\nrr = sp.sqrt((x.T*x)[0])\nur = x/rr\n\ngH = sp.simplify(\n    I-2*ur*ur.T\n)\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    (ur.T*ur)[0]-1\n) == 0\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    (ur.T*gH*ur)[0]+1\n) == 0\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    gH*gH-I\n) == sp.zeros(4)\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    sp.det(gH)+1\n) == 0\n\nprint(\n    'HOUSEHOLDER: delta(u,u)=+1 '\n    'and g(u,u)=-1; '\n    'g^2=I, det=-1, '\n    'pointwise (-+++): PASS'\n)\n\nprint(\n    'CONSTANT_FLOW: '\n    'u=(1,0,0,0), '\n    'g=diag(-1,1,1,1), '\n    'scalar curvature=0'\n)\n\n# 4. Radial Householder curvature\n\nrad,chi,theta,phi = sp.symbols(\n    'rad chi theta phi',\n    positive=True,\n    real=True\n)\n\ncoords = [rad,chi,theta,phi]\n\ng = sp.diag(\n    -1,\n    rad**2,\n    rad**2*sp.sin(chi)**2,\n    rad**2*sp.sin(chi)**2\n        *sp.sin(theta)**2\n)\n\nginv = g.inv()\nn = 4\n\nGamma = [\n    [\n        [\n            sp.simplify(\n                sum(\n                    ginv[i,k]*(\n                        sp.diff(g[k,j],coords[l])\n                        +sp.diff(g[k,l],coords[j])\n                        -sp.diff(g[j,l],coords[k])\n                    )/2\n                    for k in range(n)\n                )\n            )\n            for l in range(n)\n        ]\n        for j in range(n)\n    ]\n    for i in range(n)\n]\n\nRic = sp.MutableDenseMatrix(\n    4,4,[0]*16\n)\n\nfor i in range(n):\n    for j in range(n):\n\n        val = sum(\n            sp.diff(Gamma[k][i][j],coords[k])\n            -sp.diff(Gamma[k][i][k],coords[j])\n            +sum(\n                Gamma[k][i][j]*Gamma[l][k][l]\n                -Gamma[l][i][k]*Gamma[k][j][l]\n                for l in range(n)\n            )\n            for k in range(n)\n        )\n\n        Ric[i,j] = sp.trigsimp(\n            sp.simplify(val)\n        )\n\nscalar = sp.simplify(\n    sp.trigsimp(\n        sum(\n            ginv[i,i]*Ric[i,i]\n            for i in range(n)\n        )\n    )\n)\n\nassert Ric == sp.diag(\n    0,\n    4,\n    4*sp.sin(chi)**2,\n    4*sp.sin(chi)**2\n        *sp.sin(theta)**2\n)\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    scalar-12/rad**2\n) == 0\n\nassert sp.limit(\n    scalar,rad,sp.oo\n) == 0\n\nassert sp.limit(\n    scalar,rad,0,dir='+'\n) == sp.oo\n\nprint(\n    'RADIAL_FLOW: '\n    'ds^2=-dr^2+r^2 dOmega_3^2, '\n    'Ric=diag(0,4,4sin^2chi,'\n    '4sin^2chi sin^2theta): PASS'\n)\n\nprint(\n    'RADIAL_FLOW_SCALAR_CURVATURE: '\n    'R=12/r^2 (nonflat), '\n    'R(infty)=0, '\n    'R(0+)=infinity: PASS'\n)\n\nfor rtest in [1,2,4,10]:\n    print(\n        f'RADIAL_RICCI_SCALAR '\n        f'r={rtest}: '\n        f'{12/rtest**2:.12g}'\n    )\n\n# 5. Velocity covariance\n\nrng = np.random.default_rng(20261020)\n\nfor trial in range(500):\n\n    v = (\n        rng.normal(size=(32,4))\n        +np.array([0.,0.,0.,5.])\n    )\n\n    C = v.T@v/len(v)\n\n    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(C)\n\n    assert np.min(ev)>0\n\n    inv_ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(\n        np.linalg.inv(C)\n    )\n\n    assert np.min(inv_ev)>0\n\nprint(\n    'VELOCITY_COVARIANCE: '\n    '500 seeded full-rank trials, '\n    'C=E[vv^T] and C^-1 '\n    'positive definite: PASS'\n)\n\nv = (\n    np.ones((20,1))\n    @np.array([[0.,0.,0.,1.]])\n)\n\nassert np.linalg.matrix_rank(\n    v.T@v\n) < 4\n\nprint(\n    'COVARIANCE_RANK_DEFECT: '\n    'a perfectly aligned flow gives '\n    'singular covariance, '\n    'no ordinary inverse: PASS'\n)\n\n# 6. Quaternion double cover\n\ndef qmul(a,b):\n\n    aw,ax,ay,az = a\n    bw,bx,by,bz = b\n\n    return np.array([\n        aw*bw-ax*bx-ay*by-az*bz,\n        aw*bx+ax*bw+ay*bz-az*by,\n        aw*by-ax*bz+ay*bw+az*bx,\n        aw*bz+ax*by-ay*bx+az*bw\n    ])\n\ndef conj(q):\n    return q*np.array([1,-1,-1,-1])\n\ndef action(a,b):\n    return np.column_stack([\n        qmul(\n            qmul(a,np.eye(4)[j]),\n            conj(b)\n        )\n        for j in range(4)\n    ])\n\nmax_err = 0.\n\nfor _ in range(200):\n\n    a = rng.normal(size=4)\n    a /= np.linalg.norm(a)\n\n    b = rng.normal(size=4)\n    b /= np.linalg.norm(b)\n\n    M = action(a,b)\n    N = action(-a,-b)\n\n    err = np.max(np.abs(M-N))\n    max_err = max(max_err,err)\n\n    assert np.allclose(\n        M,N,rtol=0,atol=1e-13\n    )\n\n    assert np.allclose(\n        M.T@M,\n        np.eye(4),\n        rtol=0,\n        atol=1e-13\n    )\n\n    assert abs(\n        np.linalg.det(M)-1\n    ) < 1e-12\n\nprint(\n    'SPIN4_DOUBLE_COVER: '\n    '200 seeded cases, '\n    'same rotation for '\n    '(a,b) and (-a,-b), '\n    f'max difference {max_err:.3g}: PASS'\n)\n\nprint(\n    'GROUP_CORRECTION: '\n    'Spin(4)=SU(2)xSU(2); '\n    'SO(4)=(SU(2)xSU(2))/Z2'\n)\n\n# 7. Coarse-graining / slicing test\n\ndef pc4(a,tau,sigma,b):\n\n    spatial = (\n        a*a/(a*a+sigma*sigma)\n    )**1.5\n\n    temporal = (\n        tau/np.sqrt(tau*tau+sigma*sigma)\n    )\n\n )**1.5\n\n    return (\n        spatial\n        *np.exp(-b*b/(2*tau*tau))\n    )\n\na = tau = 1.\nsigma = .5\n\nfor b in [0.,1.,2.]:\n\n    p4 = pc4(a,tau,sigma,b)\n    p3 = c3p(a,tau,sigma,b)\n\n    print(\n        f'COARSE_GRAINING b={b:g}: '\n        f'P(C4(f))={p4:.12f}, '\n        f'C3(P(f))={p3:.12f}, '\n        f'difference={p4-p3:+.12f}'\n    )\n\nassert pc4(1,1,.5,0) < c3p(1,1,.5,0)\nassert pc4(1,1,.5,2) > c3p(1,1,.5,2)\n\nb_star = np.sqrt(\n    tau*tau\n    *(tau*tau+sigma*sigma)\n    /sigma**2\n    *np.log(\n        1+sigma*sigma/tau**2\n    )\n)\n\nassert abs(\n    pc4(a,tau,sigma,b_star)\n    -c3p(a,tau,sigma,b_star)\n) < 1e-14\n\nprint(\n    'COARSE_GRAINING_CROSSOVER: '\n    f'b_star={b_star:.12f}, '\n    'exact equality at b_star: PASS'\n)\n\n# Independent numerical quadrature\n\nmax_error = 0.\n\nfor _ in range(100):\n\n    aa,tt,ss = rng.uniform(\n        .35,2.0,size=3\n    )\n\n    bb = rng.uniform(-2.0,2.0)\n\n    spatial = (\n Exact Minkowski Frenet frame\n\nFor a timelike helix, define the normalized tangent\n\n\\[\nT=\n\\frac1d\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nb\\\\\n-r\\sin\\phi\\\\\nr\\cos\\phi\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nChoose the normal\n\n\\[\nN=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0\\\\\n-\\cos\\phi\\\\\n-\\sin\\phi\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}\n\\]\n\nand a second spacelike frame vector\n\n\\[\nB=\n\\frac1d\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nr\\\\\n-b\\sin\\phi\\\\\nb\\cos\\phi\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nThese satisfy\n\n\\[\nT\\cdot T=-1,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nN\\cdot N=B\\cdot B=1,\n\\]\n\nwith all pairwise inner products zero.\n\nDifferentiating with respect to proper spacetime length gives\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dT}{ds}=\\kappa_M N,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dN}{ds}=\\kappa_M T-\\tau_M B,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dB}{ds}=\\tau_M N.\n\\]\n\nThe resulting curvature and torsion are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa_M=\\frac{r}{b^2-r^2}\n}\n\\tag{11}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau_M=\\frac{b}{b^2-r^2}.\n}\n\\tag{12}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\tau_M^2-\\kappa_M^2\n=\n\\frac{b^2-r^2}{(b^2-r^2)^2}.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau_M^2-\\kappa_M^2\n=\n\\frac1{b^2-r^2}.\n}\n\\tag{13}\n\\]\n\nSubstituting the historical angle convention:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau_M^2-\\kappa_M^2\n=\n\\frac1{\\lambda^2\\cos(2\\theta_4)}.\n}\n\\tag{14}\n\\]\n\n**Mathematical gate: `INTERNALLY_CHECKED`.**\n\n---\n\n# 8. Exact induced metric\n\nDifferentiate Equation 12.\n\nUsing the Frenet equations,\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nF_s\n&=\nT+x(\\kappa T-\\tau B)+y\\tau N\\\\\n&=\n(1+\\kappa x)T+\\tau yN-\\tau xB.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF_s=(1+\\kappa x)T+\\tau yN-\\tau xB.\n}\n\\tag{14}\n\\]\n\nThe remaining coordinate derivatives are\n\n\\[\nF_x=N,\\qquad\nF_y=B,\\qquad\nF_z=E_z.\n\\]\n\nTheir Minkowski inner products produce the induced metric\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n-(1+\\kappa x)^2+\\tau^2(x^2+y^2)\n&\n\\tau y\n&\n-\\tau x\n&\n0\n\\\\\n\\tau y&1&0&0\\\\\n-\\tau x&0&1&0\\\\\n0&0&0&1\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\tag{15}\n\\]\n\nThis expression was constructed symbolically in SymPy.\n\n### Determinant\n\nThe determinant simplifies exactly to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\det g=-(1+\\kappa x)^2.\n}\n\\tag{16}\n\\]\n\nNotice that the torsion terms cancel.\n\nThat cancellation is significant.\n\nThe determinant depends on the curvature and the inward normal displacement, but not independently on the torsion.\n\nThe normal-coordinate map becomes locally singular when\n\n\\[\n1+\\kappa x=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx=-\\frac1\\kappa.\n}\n\\tag{17}\n\\]\n\nFor the entire three-dimensional core ball to avoid this singularity, a sufficient condition is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon\\kappa<1.\n}\n\\tag{18}\n\\]\n\nThis is a local coordinate-regularity condition.\n\nIt does not establish global injectivity, physical exclusion, or a particle-size bound.\n\n---\n\n# 7. A second threshold appears\n\nThe Frenet frame rotates.\n\nConsequently, the coordinate lines obtained by holding \\(x,y,z\\) constant while varying \\(s\\) need not remain timelike throughout the entire tube.\n\nTheir tangent norm is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng_{ss}\n=\n-(1+\\kappa x)^2\n+\n\\tau^2(x^2+y^2).\n}\n\\tag{23}\n\\]\n\nA coordinate line becomes null when\n\n\\[\ng_{ss}=0.\n\\]\n\nFor positive \\(\\kappa,\\tau\\), the earliest occurrence within a circular normal section lies at its inward radial edge:\n\n\\[\nx=-\\epsilon,\\qquad y=0.\n\\]\n\nThe null condition is\n\n\\[\n(1-\\kappa\\epsilon)^2\n=\n\\tau^2\\epsilon^2.\n\\]\n\nAt the first crossing,\n\n\\[\n1-\\kappa\\epsilon=\\tau\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon_{\\mathrm{rot}}\n=\n\\frac1{\\kappa+\\tau}.\n}\n\\tag{24}\n\\]\n\nSubstitute the Minkowski helix curvature and torsion:\n\n\\[\n\\kappa+\\tau\n=\n\\frac{r+b}{b^2-r^2}.\n\\]\n\nFactor the denominator:\n\n\\[\nb^2-r^2=(b-r)(b+r).\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\kappa+\\tau=\\frac1{b-r}.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon_{\\mathrm{rot}}=b-r.\n}\n\\tag{25}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact identity.\n\nUnder the historical parametrization,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon_{\\mathrm{rot}}\n=\n\\lambda(\\cos\\theta_4-\\sin\\theta_4).\n}\n\\tag{26}\n\\]\n\nThe rotating-frame coordinate lines become null at a smaller core radius than the radius at which the normal-coordinate map itself becomes singular.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Why the second threshold is not intrinsic\n\nWe can test whether the additional threshold survives a change of frame.\n\nConstruct a nonrotating Fermi-Walker frame:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_1=\n\\cos(\\tau s)N+\\sin(\\tau s)B\n}\n\\tag{27}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_2=\n-\\sin(\\tau s)N+\\cos(\\tau s)B.\n}\n\\tag{28}\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate.\n\nThe torsion terms cancel:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_1'=\\kappa\\cos(\\tau s)T\n}\n\\tag{29}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_2'=-\\kappa\\sin(\\tau s)T.\n}\n\\tag{30}\n\\]\n\nNow construct\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF_{\\mathrm{FW}}(s,u,v,z)\n=\nX(s)+uE_1(s)+vE_2(s)+zE_z.\n}\n\\tag{31}\n\\]\n\nThe time-coordinate derivative becomes\n\n\\[\nF_{\\mathrm{FW},s}\n=\n\\left[\n1+\\kappa\n\\left(\nu\\cos(\\tau s)-v\\sin(\\tau s)\n\\right)\n\\right]T.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng_{ss}^{\\mathrm{FW}}\n=\n-\n\\left[\n1+\\kappa\n\\left(\nu\\cos(\\tau s)-v\\sin(\\tau s)\n\\right)\n\\right]^2.\n}\n\\tag{32}\n\\]\n\nThe shift terms vanish:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng_{su}=g_{sv}=g_{sz}=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe additional torsion-dependent null-coordinate-line condition has disappeared.\n\nThe local coordinate singularity remains controlled by the curvature.\n\nThus the two thresholds have different meanings.\n\n| Condition | Radius | Interpretation |\n|---|---|---|\n| Rotating Frenet coordinate lines become null | \\(b-r\\) | Frame-dependent coordinate-flow property |\n| Normal-coordinate Jacobian becomes singular | \\((b^2-r^2)/r\\) | Local regularity limit of the normal map |\n\nNeither is automatically a physical boundary.\n\n### Numerical comparison\n\nFor \\(\\lambda=1\\):\n\n| \\(\\theta_4\\) | Rotating-frame radius | Local map radius |\n|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1° | 0.982395 | 57.263784 |\n| 15° | 0.707107 | 3.346065 |\n| 30° | 0.366025 | 1.000000 |\n| 40° | 0.123257 | 0.270149 |\n| 44° | 0.024681 | 0.050240 |\n\n![Rotating-frame versus local-map thresholds](sandbox:/mnt/data/sable_20261020t0812/classP_frame_comparison.png)\n\nThe distinction becomes especially clear near the straight-worldline limit.\n\nAs\n\n\\[\n\\theta_4\\rightarrow0^+,\n\\]\n\nthe curvature tends to zero.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon_{\\mathrm{local}}\\rightarrow\\infty.\n\\]\n\nBut the rotating-frame threshold approaches\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon_{\\mathrm{rot}}\\rightarrow\\lambda.\n\\]\n\nThe finite rotating-frame threshold persists solely because the chosen frame continues rotating in the limiting construction.\n\nIt is not an intrinsic curvature constraint.\n\n**This is the strongest result of the turn.**\n\n---\n\n# 10.
